headlines.title: Caltrans reschedules lane closure on Carquinez Bridge
headlines.description: A lane closure previously scheduled for this weekend on the westbound Carquinez Bridge has been rescheduled for the following weekend, according to Caltrans. The one-lane closure on Interstate 80 will take place Aug. 14 at 6 p.m. through Aug. 15 at 7 p.m. Caltrans said in a statement that the closure is due to construction for the agency’s ongoing bridge deck rehabilitation project. A full closure of the westbound Carquinez Bridge is planned for Aug. 21-24. Caltrans is hosting a public meeting to discuss construction plans on Monday at 6 p.m. at the Norman C. King South Vallejo Community Center at 545 Magazine St. in Vallejo. The pedestrian and bike path will remain open during the lane closure. For updates, visit 511.org and quickmap.dot.ca.gov.

headlines.title: Court orders Instagram and Facebook's Meta to pay $567M to address kids' mental health online
headlines.description: A New Mexico court has ordered Instagram and Facebook parent company Meta to pay $567 million to address harms to young people from its platforms in the second phase of a landmark trial. Judge Bryan Biedscheid said in a ruling late Thursday that the bulk of the money — $420 million — will be used for treatment services for young people. The rest will go toward awareness and prevention, screening services and other costs over the next five years. The new penalty is in addition to the $375 million in civil penalties that jurors ordered against Meta in March after determining the company knowingly harmed children’s mental health and concealed what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms. In the second phase, prosecutors asked the judge to impose fundamental changes at Meta aimed at reining in addictive features, improving age verification and preventing child sexual exploitation through default privacy settings and closer oversight. The total amount Meta is responsible for — $942 million — is a small fraction of of its annual profit, which was about $60 billion in 2025. Investors seemed to shrug off the New Mexico ruling in after-hours trading Thursday, sending Meta’s stock down less than half a percent to $589.44. Still, the ruling is another setback for Meta, which faces an avalanche of lawsuits from thousands of families of children harmed by social media. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said it sends an unmistakable message that companies will be held accountable when their product designs knowingly put children at risk. “Today’s decision is a victory for every parent who has worried about what social media is doing to their child and every child who deserves to grow up safer online,” he said in a statement. Meta vowed to appeal. “We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content,” the company said in a statement. “We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts.” The look of Meta’s platforms could change The judge ordered Facebook and Instagram to build banner and informational screens to clearly explain its protection features, best practices and tools to address inappropriate comment, for example, and display them regularly. Those changes and an educational campaign in New Mexico would be subject to review by the state. The court said federal children’s privacy laws prevent Meta from applying age-verification tools to children under 13. The Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA, means it cannot order Meta to request children to submit personal data or be passively tracked online, even for age verification purposes. The court also noted that ordering verification of children’s ages only for Meta and not other social media companies would be “inequitable and unduly injurious” to the company. Instead, the court ordered Meta to continue to improve its age assurance tools in New Mexico, which include using artificial intelligence to determine people’s age based on signals such as who their friends are and what types of content they post and consume. Meta must also attempt to develop a dedicated “under-13-years-of-age prediction model” in the next two years. Additionally, Meta should also request proof of age for Instagram and Facebook users in New Mexico it estimates to be under 13. If it determines a user to be under 13, or under 18 but without being able to estimate a specific age, Meta must treat the user as under 13 or under 18 until the user verifies their age. The company must also partner with schools or a child safety organization to create a reporting portal where school staff can flag users who may be under 13. And it must delete personal information it has collected on users under 13. The court also ordered Meta to report on its progress twice a year on how it’s complying with the abatement measures. Meta is gearing up for a trial this month in California amid flood of lawsuits Meta is also gearing up for a trial later this month in federal court in Oakland, California. Here, Meta will face the first four of 29 states that sued it in a federal multi-district lawsuit filed in 2023 for contributing to the youth mental health crisis by knowingly designing features on Instagram and Facebook that addict children to its platforms. Eight states, including Tennessee, where a trial is currently ongoing, filed lawsuits in their own state courts. And late last month, Meta, along with TikTok, Snap and Google’s YouTube, were sued by the families of four teenagers who died by suicide over what they describe as “years of escalating harms” from using their platforms that eventually resulted in their deaths. What comes out of New Mexico is the first of many dominoes that will fall for Meta, said Laura Edelson, an assistant professor at Northeastern University focusing on social media and cybersecurity. “America is not going to pass a law that bans social media,” Edelson said. “But if companies like Meta know they’re causing harm to users by product design, the states are finally finding a way to rein this in.” ____ This story has been updated to correct the judge’s last name to Biedscheid, not Biedcheid. ___ Ortutay reported from Oakland, California, and Yu from Phoenix. Associated Press writer Mikella Schuettler in Phoenix contributed. Schuettler is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.
headlines.source: Barbara Ortutay | The Associated Press and Wufei Yu | The Associated Press

headlines.title: Earth, Wind & Fire concert in San Francisco canceled due to medical emergency
headlines.description: Thursday’s Earth, Wind & Fire concert in San Francisco was canceled due to a medical emergency involving a band member, according to officials. According to a statement released by Chase Center, the show with Lionel Richie was postponed after an Earth, Wind & Fire band member had a medical emergency. The city’s fire department said they received a medical call to Chase Center at around 5:30 p.m., and one person was transported to the hospital via private ambulance. Chase Center and the band encourage fans to hold to their tickets since those will be honored for the new date, or “refunds will be available at the point of purchase.” “Earth, Wind & Fire is unable to perform as scheduled tonight due to a medical emergency involving a member of their band,” the band wrote on social media. “As a result, tonight’s show with Lionel Richie will be rescheduled, with a new date to be announced soon. Ticket holders should retain their tickets, which will be honored for the new date, or refunds will be available at the point of purchase. We sincerely apologize for the unexpected change and appreciate everyone’s understanding.”

headlines.title: United flight returns to SFO after blowing tire during departure
headlines.description: A United Airlines flight returned safely to San Francisco International Airport Thursday after blowing a tire during departure, the FAA said. United Flight 1189, a Boeing 737-800 bound for Los Cabos International Airport in Mexico, landed back at SFO at about 11:45 a.m., according to the FAA. Footage from NBC Bay Area SkyRanger showed people exiting the plane via stairs – while the aircraft was still on the tarmac – and getting onto buses to return to the terminal. The plane was carrying 165 passengers and eight crew members, United said. No injuries were reported. United said it arranged for a different plane to take the passengers to Los Cabos later Thursday afternoon. The FAA said it will conduct an investigation.

headlines.title: Rodeo rides into Gilroy this weekend
headlines.description: The Gilroy Rodeo returns this weekend, with the three-day event sold out. The annual event dates back to 1930 and will feature rodeo competitions, entertainment and family-friendly activities. Organizers say the weekend celebration continues to honor Gilroy’s ranching heritage while welcoming visitors from across the Bay Area. NBC Bay Area’s Ali Reid has more in the video above.

headlines.title: Senior tenants from Oakland protest housing conditions, lobby state officials
headlines.description: More than 20 seniors traveled by bus to Sacramento Thursday to protest the conditions at their East Oakland affordable housing complex and implore state officials to take enforcement action against their landlords and property managers. As NBC Bay Area recently reported, dozens of tenants living in the Oakland Station apartments allege the building is filthy and infested with cockroaches. They also say the building is unsafe – especially for its senior tenants – with frequent elevator outages and a broken security gate that allows anyone to come inside. Last month, more than 60 current and former tenants filed a lawsuit against the building’s owners and management company, alleging a long list of civil violations, including elder abuse and harassment. On Thursday, they took the fight to the doorstep of their property management company, CONAM, protesting outside the company’s Roseville office. “Roaches, trash everywhere, dog poop and people poop, safety hazards…” said tenant Cathy Harris, rattling off a list of concerns through a megaphone. Another tenant, Isabelle Ruiz, held up a jar of roaches – now dead – calling it a small sample of the infestation in her apartment. “I have my new roommates with me that I’ve brought in to show everyone,” Ruiz said. The tenants have been organizing with the help of community organizers at ACCE. “We came to CONAM because they have not been hearing us,” said Valarie Bachelor, the nonprofit’s Oakland director. “We need our units fixed.” NBC Bay Area reached out to CONAM after the protest for comment but has not yet received a response. Neither CONAM nor the building’s owners have commented in two previous NBC Bay Area stories on tenant concerns. While in Sacramento, the tenants and organizers also met with state officials with the California Tax Credit Allocation Committee, asking them to take enforcement action against their landlords. “They are not maintaining the building and they’re disrespecting us and we’re living in squalor,” one tenant said. The tenants allege in their lawsuit that the building’s owners received millions-of-dollars’ worth of low-income housing tax credits for developing affordable housing but let the building fall apart in just five years.

headlines.title: CA 988 mental health tech is years overdue, linked to troubled Next Gen 911 upgrade
headlines.description: In 2019, 23-year-old Miles Hall was suffering from mental illness when he was shot and killed by police in Walnut Creek. Officers said he ran towards them with a metal pole gardening tool. “We had already known Miles had schizophrenia. He had a delusion and thought this garden tool was a staff from God,” his mother Taun Hall said. “Miles [was] trying to go home.” Even though the Contra Costa County District Attorney’s Office found the officers acted in self-defense, Hall’s death helped pass Assembly Bill 988. Miles Hall’s death in 2019 helped inspire Assembly Bill 988. The law required expanded mental health services through the state’s suicide hotline number 988 – an alternative to 911 meant to divert mental health victims away from law enforcement. Currently, if you dial 988 you’ll reach a crisis center where workers are trained to support and de-escalate. But there’s a problem. Many people in a mental health crisis still call 911 or have 911 called on them. In California, there are about 25 million 911 calls every year. About 30% involve some sort of mental health component, according to Narges Dillion, president of the 988 California Consortium and executive director of Crisis Support Services of Alameda County. “If we think about even 1% of those callers really being better served transitioning to a 988 center, we’re talking about 260,000. Those are real people,” Dillon said. To address this problem, another part of AB 988 required the California Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES) to create a statewide system where operators can seamlessly transfer emergency calls between 988 and 911. The state has spent $24.5 million on this project so far that was originally budgeted for $7.6 million for fiscal year 2022/2023. It’s also two years overdue. Cal OES’ 988 project has cost $24.5M so far and is two years overdue. “Instead of us being able invest that funding into the centers to expand our capacity, the funding is going towards technology or a broader system that no one knows what’s happening with. That lack of accountability I think is concerning at multiple levels,” Dillon said. In Sacramento, lawmakers and experts at Steinberg Institute are scrutinizing Cal OES. “How has California fallen so far behind on progress on a federally mandated program with dedicated funding, broad stakeholder support and overwhelming public need?” said Tara Eastman with Steinberg Institute at a recent hearing. That answer, the Investigative Unit found, has to do with another Cal OES project: The Next Generation 911 upgrade that our team of journalists has been exposing for two years now for major cost overruns, and misrouted and dropped 911 calls. The two projects are linked. The 988 technology can’t move forward until the Next Gen 911 network is deployed, which could be another 4 years, according to a recent legislative outcomes review. Cal OES declined an interview with NBC Bay Area but said in a statement, “Every Californian experiencing a mental health crisis deserves to be connected quickly to the right help… Today, every 9-8-8 center can transfer calls to another 9-8-8 center or connect callers directly with a 9-1-1 dispatch center when emergency assistance is needed.” Narges Dillon (left) and Candice Nguyen (right). The agency said the transfer connections have been validated and meet state law requirements. However, that transfer capability is far from what proponents of AB 988 envisions, lawmakers found. There’s only “baseline interoperability” that already existed with the old legacy technology, they said in the legislative outcomes review. Cal OES said it has built an upgraded transfer platform that appears to be working, but only a pilot version is being used at one of California’s 11 crisis centers. “We repeatedly feel like we’re not a priority,” said Dillon. “As more an dmore people are asking us for help.” Taun Hall feels that it is wrong that 911 dispatchers didn’t have the right tools to get her son the services he needed in 2019. She feels it’s wrong that all those tools still aren’t available. “Any moment that it is delayed could be a life that is lost, like Miles,” she said. Candice Nguyen is the senior investigative reporter on this story. If you have a question about this story or an investigation tip, email her at candice.nguyen@nbcuni.com.

headlines.title: Children under 10 crash car into pedestrian in Oakland, sending woman to hospital
headlines.description: Two children under the age of 10 took a car belonging to one of their parents Thursday and later struck a pedestrian in Oakland, leaving her in critical condition, police said. The collision happened at about 9:30 a.m. in the area of 35th and Mangels avenues, not far from Interstate 580, according to police. Police said the pedestrian, a woman in her 30s, was taken to a hospital. The two children, who sources said are 6 and 4 years old, were also taken to a hospital and listed in stable condition. Witness Anthony Hudson said multiple people ran to help the woman, performing CPR until paramedics arrived. “It was just tragic,” Hudson said. The kids appeared to be traveling northbound on 35th Avenue when they hit another vehicle traveling in the opposite direction, causing them to lose control and hit the pedestrian as she was walking with a dog in a crosswalk, according to police. Witnesses said the dog appeared to be OK. Witnesses, shocked at the ages of the children in the car, said the kids were lying on the ground with injuries and appeared to be in shock after the crash. The parents of the children were cooperating with the investigation. It wasn’t immediately known if alcohol and/or drugs played a role, police said. An investigation is ongoing. Oakland Aug 5 Oakland Aug 2 Oakland Aug 1

headlines.title: Arrest made in 6-alarm fire at Foster City condominium complex
headlines.description: A Foster City resident was arrested in connection with a six-alarm blaze that ripped through a condominium complex and left four firefighters injured last weekend, police said Thursday. Keith Tompkins was arrested for unlawfully causing a fire resulting in injury to firefighters; obstructing and delaying a police investigation; and willfully resisting, obstructing, or delaying a fire investigation, according to police. The blaze at the Spinnaker Cove condominium complex at 815 Sea Spray Ln. sparked Sunday afternoon and raged for several hours. Four firefighters were injured but are expected to be OK. Everyone was rescued, but the flames spread across roughly 50 units in the building, which was built in the 1980s and, according to residents, had no sprinklers. Investigators determined the blaze was caused by an unattended gas grill on an exterior balcony. Tompkins was taken into custody without incident and booked into the San Mateo County Jail, police said. He later posted bond and was released on Wednesday. In a phone call with Tompkins on Thursday, he told NBC Bay Area that things are difficult right now, adding that he wasn’t sure if he should talk. Tompkins previously spoke to NBC Bay Area a few times outside the burned condos. Prosecutors on Thursday said they didn’t have the case file yet, but the district attorney confirmed the arrest and will wait while the police investigation continues. Foster City Aug 3 Foster City Aug 2 4 firefighters injured in six-alarm fire at Foster City condominium complex

headlines.title: Pedestrian killed in collision on southbound Highway 85 in San Jose
headlines.description: A pedestrian was killed early Thursday morning after being struck by a vehicle on southbound Highway 85 in San Jose, according to the California Highway Patrol. The crash was reported shortly after 1:30 a.m. near the Camden Avenue off-ramp. Patrol officers temporarily stopped all southbound traffic and diverted vehicles onto the Camden Avenue off-ramp. It was later reopened, and all lanes were back open by 3:50 a.m., according to the CHP. No further information about the crash was immediately available

headlines.title: Community gathers to discuss toxic chemicals found under Richmond school campus
headlines.description: On Thursday, parents, students and community members gathered at Richmond City Hall to hear directly from the school district, city officials and scientists with the Department of Toxic Substances Control following the discovery of toxic chemicals under a high school campus. Scientists say the state has been testing the soil under streets in Richmond over the past few years. They discovered contamination under the street 500 feet from campus; that’s when they decided to test the soil at campus. They tested six locations within school grounds and found levels of tetrachloroethylene, or pce, at five of those locations along cutting and 45th. They are now sampling the air to see the toxic chemicals have become airborne. Those results are expected on Aug.12. They’ll be analyzed on Aug. 13 and Aug. 14 and then a decision will be made whether allow students to attend school at Kennedy High or move class elsewhere.

headlines.title: Annual Silicon Valley Pain Index findings released
headlines.description: Researchers at San Jose State University on Thursday revealed this year’s index on economic inequality in Silicon Valley. The Silicon Valley Pain Index, a report put together by SJSU’s Human Rights Institute, evaluates societal needs such as housing, food and childcare. The goal is to inform government, community leaders and the public of persistent inequalities in areas including employment, education, housing, population, health and overall well-being. The index shows that the top 10% of residents hold 75% of the area’s wealth. The bottom 50% of residents hold less than 1%. “We have an even greater gap in income between the wealthiest and the rest of us,” lead author Anji Buckner-Capone said. “We have seen more schools close. We have seen increases in compromised physical and mental health. We have far too many individuals and families who are unsure how they will make ends meet.” According to the index, San Jose ranks as one of the most expensive large cities in the United States. To buy a standard home, citizens need an income of over $460,000. “We have abundant resources,” The Health Trust CEO Dr. Tony Iton said. “There’s enough for everybody to get food and healthcare and childcare. It’s not like there are shortages of these things. It’s just the policy is not investing in our people.”
